passage:
Tuesday
Mohit got 4 out of 20 in his spelling test. I saw it in his bag. At dinner I said, "Papa, guess who got FOUR?" and laughed. Papa looked at me, and I thought he'd say I was the good one. But he just rubbed his eyes and said, "Not now, Divyansh."
Later I told Mummy that Mohit hid the test. I thought she would be pleased with me. She just sighed.
Mohit didn't talk to me all evening. When I went to sleep he had turned his back. He whispered, "I'll never tell you anything again."
I thought I'd feel like the winner. I don't.
Divyansh

qa.q: What did Mohit get in his spelling test?
qa.a: He got 4 out of 20.

qa.q: What did Divyansh want when telling on Mohit?
qa.a: Divyansh wanted Papa and Mummy to see Divyansh as the good one and be pleased.

qa.q: What could Divyansh do next time he finds out about Mohit's mistake?
qa.a: He could keep it private or even offer to help with spelling, instead of mocking or reporting, so Mohit can trust Divyansh again.

qa.q: How does Mohit feel after the dinner?
qa.a: He feels hurt and betrayed, which is why he turned his back and said he'd never tell Divyansh anything again.

grounding: It shows a child mocking a brother's failure and telling on him to win a parent's approval, leaving a tired parent and a brother with a real grievance.

passage: Evening in the village, and Sharmila had just come back from the fields, her feet dusty and her back aching. Before she could sit, Minakshi ran up. "Amma! Madhu broke the pot at the well and he fell in the mud, he looked so silly!" She laughed and flapped her arms like him falling. "And he didn't do his homework!" Madhu stood behind the door, his face red. Sharmila closed her eyes. "Minakshi, enough." Minakshi's smile faded. She had expected Amma to say, good girl for telling. Madhu glared at her and went to the back of the house. He didn't call her for their usual game of stones that night.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say Madhu broke?
qa.a: She said he broke the pot at the well.

qa.q: What did Minakshi expect when she told Amma?
qa.a: She hoped Amma would praise her as a good girl for telling, so she felt let down when Amma said 'enough' and her smile faded.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Mocking and reporting Madhu only tired Amma and hurt Madhu; Minakshi could say sorry to Madhu, and Amma could later talk to each child calmly and separately.

qa.q: How does Madhu feel after being mocked in front of Amma?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and angry, so he glares at his sister and skips their usual game of stones.

grounding: It illustrates a child mocking her brother and telling on him to gain adult favour, which only wearies the parent and gives the brother a real grievance.

passage:
Sarita wobbled on the new cycle in the village lane, then fell into the dust for the third time.

Her brother Vishal laughed loudly. "Look, she can't even ride! Baby! Baby!"

Sarita's lip trembled. She threw a pebble at him.

Vishal ran straight to the kitchen. "Amma! Sarita threw a stone at me!"

Amma was frying puris, sweat on her forehead. "Both of you, stop it!"

"But she started—"

"Vishal, you laughed at her. I heard." Amma turned back to the pan, tired.

Vishal went outside. Sarita wasn't speaking to him now. And Amma hadn't taken his side at all.

qa.q: How many times did Sarita fall off the cycle?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why did Vishal run to tell Amma?
qa.a: He hoped to win Amma's favour and get Sarita in trouble, after mocking her for falling.

qa.q: What went wrong for Vishal, and what could he try instead?
qa.a: Mocking and tattling left Amma tired and Sarita angry; he could help Sarita learn to ride instead.

qa.q: How does Sarita feel after being laughed at?
qa.a: She feels hurt and humiliated, then angry enough to throw a pebble and stop speaking to Vishal.

grounding: Vishal mocks his sister's failure and runs to tell on her to win his mother's favour, but both lose as Amma is tired and Sarita now has a real grievance.

passage:
In their flat in Izmir, Zeynep's brother Emir got a low mark on his spelling test and hid the paper under his bed.

Zeynep found it. She waved it in the air. "Emir got four out of twenty! Four!"

Emir went red. "Give it back!"

She didn't. She ran to their mother, who was paying bills at the table. "Anne, Emir hid his test!"

Their mother sighed and rubbed her eyes. "Zeynep, why are you telling me this now?"

Emir stood in the doorway, glaring at his sister. Later, he took her favourite pen and wouldn't give it back.

Now they were both in trouble, and their mother was even more tired.

qa.q: What mark did Emir get on his spelling test?
qa.a: Four out of twenty.

qa.q: What did Zeynep hope to gain by running to their mother?
qa.a: She hoped to win her mother's approval and make Emir look bad.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Zeynep have done instead?
qa.a: Tattling made their mother more tired and gave Emir a real grievance; Zeynep could have kept quiet or encouraged Emir to tell himself.

qa.q: How does Emir feel after his sister waves his test around?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and angry, and takes revenge by keeping her favourite pen.

grounding: Zeynep mocks her brother's low mark and tells on him to gain favour, but it tires their mother and gives Emir a real grievance.

passage:
At the school in Kanpur, Hemant saw his younger brother Varun get out in the first over of the house cricket match. Hemant laughed with his friends. "Duck! Varun got a duck!"

Varun's ears went pink.

At lunch Varun marched to the staffroom. "Sir, Hemant was laughing at me and saying bad words!"

Hemant hadn't said any bad words. Mr Joshi, busy marking forty notebooks, called both brothers in.

"Hemant, did you laugh at him?"

"...Yes."

"Varun, did he say bad words?"

"...No."

Mr Joshi rubbed his forehead. "Both of you, sit here till the bell."

Neither of them got what he wanted.

qa.q: How did Varun get out?
qa.a: In the first over of the house cricket match, for a duck.

qa.q: Why did Varun go to the staffroom and exaggerate?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry after being laughed at, and wanted the teacher to take his side against Hemant.

qa.q: What could each brother have done instead?
qa.a: Hemant could have cheered Varun up instead of mocking, and Varun could have said honestly that he felt hurt.

qa.q: How might Mr Joshi feel dealing with this?
qa.a: He is tired and busy, and frustrated to spend lunch sorting out both brothers' mocking and exaggeration.

grounding: Hemant mocks his brother's failure and Varun tattles with an exaggeration to win the teacher's favour, and both lose.

passage:
Monday. Varun dropped the catch in the colony cricket match. At dinner Swati giggled, "Butterfingers Varun!" Mummy smiled a little, and Swati felt pleased.
Wednesday. Swati saw Varun eat a biscuit before homework. She ran to the kitchen. "Mummy, Varun's eating biscuits and he hasn't finished maths!" Mummy sighed "Varun!" from the stove. Varun glared at Swati all evening.
Saturday. Swati ran in again. "Mummy, Varun..." Mummy, rubbing her forehead, said, "Swati, not now. I'm so tired of this." Swati's smile vanished. That night Varun hid her favourite pencil box and wouldn't say where. "You always get me in trouble," he said. Nobody had won anything.

qa.q: What did Varun drop in the colony cricket match?
qa.a: Varun dropped the catch.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when Mummy smiled at 'Butterfingers Varun'?
qa.a: Swati felt pleased and proud, as if teasing Varun had won Mummy's favour.

qa.q: What could Swati try instead of running to Mummy?
qa.a: She could leave small things like the biscuit alone and fetch an adult only for real safety problems, which would keep the peace with Varun.

qa.q: How does Varun see Swati's tattling by Saturday?
qa.a: Varun feels he is always being got into trouble, so he holds a real grievance and hits back by hiding her pencil box.

grounding: Shows a child teasing and telling on a sibling to win a parent's favour, leaving a tired parent and a sibling with a real grievance.
